paras: The West End mob letter to M. E. McKelley was an anonymous written order, dated August 23, 1903, telling the only Black family living on the West Side of Wichita, Kansas, to leave within ten days. McKelley decided, on the advice of local business men, not to move, and police detectives were reported searching for the writer.

M. E. McKelley, described by the Wichita Daily Eagle as "a colored man employed by the street railway company," lived at 914 West Douglas avenue and had been on the West Side since the previous spring. He had lived in Wichita twelve or fifteen years earlier, working at the Crystal ice plant and the Wichita steam laundry before going to Nebraska. According to the Eagle, one Black family had lived on the West Side for years, and none had been ordered away before.

The letter, headed "West Wichita, Aug 23, 1903" and addressed to "Mr. McKelly," told him that he was "the only black family on this side and we dont allow such people here." It warned that he would not be given more than ten days to get out and was signed "West End mob / grasshopper Ike in Command." The Eagle noted that it was written in lead pencil on cheap note paper, with poor handwriting, no punctuation and few capitals.

Many West Side people were shown the letter, and the Eagle reported that it caused "considerable surprise" among business men, who advised him to stay. While some readers treated it as a joke, the paper said McKelley was "pretty well scared" and that he and his wife did not think it was written in fun. The letter was given to the police, whose detectives were trying to find the writer; no report of an arrest appears in the coverage.

The only known report is a page-five story in the Wichita Daily Eagle of August 28, 1903, headlined "ORDER TO MOVE FROM WEST SIDE" with the subheads "Colored Man Received Anonymous Letter" and "TEN DAYS IS THE LIMIT." The Eagle printed the letter in full as "verbatim," stressed the neighbors' surprise, and gave weight to McKelley's fear alongside those who called it a joke. No coverage in the Black press or in other white papers was found, and no follow-up report on the case was found.
